title: Investing in Why People Stay Instead of Worrying About Why They Might Leave
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues retention strategy should focus on why top performers stay rather than reactively negotiating counteroffers when they receive outside interest, which the author calls a defensive, slippery-slope tactic. Beyond the direct relationship with a manager, the piece identifies four reasons talented people stay -- feeling challenged, feeling valued by senior leaders, finding the vision compelling, and experiencing consistent investment in their skill development -- and argues investment in skills creates the strongest retention glue of all. It closes by describing organizations that invest in talent development as 'stickier' than those that don't.
points: Negotiating counteroffers in reaction to outside offers is a slippery slope -- word gets out, and people start seeking outside offers just to leverage their status.
Going on offense means asking why the best people stay, not just tracking who's at risk of leaving.
Four retention drivers beyond the direct manager relationship: feeling challenged, feeling valued by senior leaders, a compelling vision, and consistent investment in skill development.
Investment in people's skills is described as the strongest retention glue because it creates a sense of reciprocal loyalty.
quotes: But offering more compensation or a better title in reaction to an outside offer is a slippery slope.
Focusing on why people may leave is a sensible strategy, but a defensive one. It is better to go on offense.

The most talented team members stay put for four reasons: they feel challenged by the work they do, they feel valued by the most senior leaders in the organization, they find the vision of the organization compelling, and they feel the organization is consistently investing in their skill development.
It is the investment in people’s skills that often creates the strongest glue.
An organization that is devoted to improving talent is an enterprise that is stickier than others.
